unit.title: The paddock: who does what
unit.summary: Team roles, radio, teammates, the driver pipeline and the media world.

lessons.title: Who runs a team
lessons.objective: Explain what the principal, engineer and strategist each do.

payload.prompt: Match each team role to what they do.

pairs.definition: The boss who runs the team, its budget and the public face to sponsors and media.
The driver's main voice on radio: coaches the driver and relays set-up and strategy.
Where strategists sit trackside, reading data and making live race calls.

distractorDefinitions: The driver who leads the team in points.
The team's safety officer during pit stops.

explanation.summary: A team is three layers: the boss (principal), the driver's engineer (on radio), and the strategists (trackside data). Each has a clear job.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three jobs: the principal runs it, the engineer coaches the driver, the pit wall reads the race.

payload.prompt: What is the team principal's main job?

options.text: Running the team, the budget, and the team's image with sponsors and media.
options.explanation: Right. The principal is the boss and the public face.

options.text: Deciding pit stops and strategy calls during the race.
options.explanation: That is the pit wall and the engineer. The principal runs the team, not the race.

options.text: Driving the second car if the main driver is injured.
options.explanation: That is the reserve driver's job, not the principal's.

options.text: Tuning the car set-up before qualifying.
options.explanation: The engineer tunes the car. The principal runs the team.

explanation.correct: Right. The principal is the boss and the public face of the team to sponsors, media and the FIA.
explanation.incorrect: The team principal runs the team and its budget; they do not make race decisions or drive. That is the engineer and reserve driver.
explanation.sayThisLine: The principal runs the team; the engineer runs the race.

payload.prompt: Who is the driver's everyday voice on the radio?

scene.alt: Text only: two candidates for the person who talks to the driver during a race.

explanation.correct: The race engineer knows the car, reads the data and passes on set-up and strategy. Drivers trust one familiar voice, so that is who you hear.
explanation.incorrect: The principal runs the whole team and rarely speaks on the radio. The driver's everyday voice is the race engineer, who relays what the pit wall decides.
explanation.sayThisLine: The engineer is the driver's coach on the radio.

payload.prompt: What do strategists on the pit wall do?

options.text: Read live data, watch the race, and make strategy calls: when to pit, when to save, what to do under yellows.
options.explanation: Right. The pit wall is the strategy brain, reading the race second by second.

options.text: Build and repair the car in the garage.
options.explanation: That is the mechanics' job. The pit wall is on the strategy side.

options.text: Drive the pace car if a safety car is needed.
options.explanation: The race director and FIA run safety cars; the pit wall is for strategy.

options.text: Broadcast the race on television.
options.explanation: Broadcasters work for the media; the pit wall is a team function.

explanation.correct: Right. The pit wall watches the race, reads data and tyre wear, and calls the shots: pit, stay out, how to manage the gap.
explanation.incorrect: The pit wall is the race control centre for one team: data, strategy and live decision-making.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pit wall reads the race and calls strategy in real time.

payload.prompt: Match each term to what it means in the team.

pairs.definition: The driver's closest adviser: knows the car, coaches on strategy and is the single radio voice.
The trackside team who watch data, weather and other cars to guide strategy.
The team boss: runs the business, sets budgets and speaks to sponsors and media.

distractorDefinitions: The chief mechanic who oversees all pit-stop crews.
The FIA official who monitors team radio for rule breaks.

explanation.summary: Three leaders: the principal runs the team as a business; the engineer coaches the driver; the pit wall guides strategy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Principal = boss. Engineer = coach. Pit wall = strategist.

lessons.title: Reading team radio
lessons.objective: Decode common radio messages and what is really being said.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: The radio just said box box. Are they in trouble?

payload.question: What does box box mean?

options.text: It is the pit call: come into the pits this lap, usually for new tyres.
options.explanation: Exactly. Box box is a routine instruction to pit, most often planned and most often for tyres.

options.text: The driver should stay out a little longer than planned.
options.explanation: That is the opposite. Stay out is the call for not pitting yet.

options.text: The car has a serious problem and must stop for good.
options.explanation: Damage or a fault gets its own message. Box box on its own is a normal pit call.

payload.translation: Box box means the driver should come into the pit lane this lap. It is usually a planned tyre stop, not a crisis.

followUps.line: Is it always for new tyres?
followUps.why: Mostly, because refuelling has been banned since 2010. A stop can also be for a repair, like a broken wing.

followUps.line: Do they say it twice on purpose?
followUps.why: Yes. Repeating it makes it clear on a noisy radio, so the driver cannot miss it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Box box is not an emergency. If you are unsure why they boxed, ask what tyre they went on to.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: He is lifting and coasting, trying to save fuel and energy.

payload.question: What does lifting and coasting mean?

options.text: The driver comes off the throttle early before braking to save fuel, energy or brakes.
options.explanation: Right. It costs a little lap time now in exchange for saving something for later.

options.text: The driver is taking it easy because the race is boring.
options.explanation: It is never about boredom. It is a deliberate instruction from the pit wall.

options.text: The car has run out of fuel and is rolling to a stop.
options.explanation: Lifting and coasting is planned and the car keeps racing. Running dry is a different, much worse radio call.

payload.translation: Lifting and coasting means getting off the throttle earlier than normal before a braking zone, trading a little lap time for fuel, battery or brake savings.

followUps.line: Who tells him when to do it?
followUps.why: Usually the engineer, based on the team's fuel or energy numbers and what the cars behind are doing.

followUps.line: Why not just go flat out?
followUps.why: The race is long. Saving a little each lap can be the difference between finishing strong and being slow at the end.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is a tactical choice, not weakness. If you do not know why he is doing it, ask what he is saving.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: You should hear what they say on the radio. It is hilarious and sometimes angry.

payload.question: Why do people love team radio?

options.text: It is raw emotion and real strategy talk: frustration, funny moments, and actual racing decisions unscripted.
options.explanation: Right. Team radio is real-time drama and a window into the race.

options.text: It is just the engineer giving pit calls.
options.explanation: It is more than pit calls. It is emotion, jokes, damage reports, complaints, praise.

options.text: It is boring technical talk that fans would not understand.
options.explanation: Some is technical, but fans love the raw drama and humour of real drivers.

payload.translation: Team radio is the unscripted chatter between the driver and engineer during the race: pit calls, strategy, emotion and humour.

followUps.line: Do they edit the radio for TV?
followUps.why: Yes. F1 broadcasts only radio that is interesting or relevant to the race. Beeping censors profanity.

followUps.line: Can a driver get in trouble for what they say on the radio?
followUps.why: Sometimes. The FIA can investigate unsportsmanlike or insulting language, but plain frustration is fine.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Team radio is a real thing to listen to; it helps you follow the race and feel the human side.

payload.template: {{pit}} tells the driver to come in, and {{stay}} tells them to keep going.

explanation.correct: Box box is the call to pit this lap. Stay out means the plan is to keep running, often to wait for a better window.
explanation.incorrect: Box box means pit this lap. Stay out means do not pit yet. Push now is about pace, not about pitting.
explanation.sayThisLine: They said stay out, so the stop is coming later.

lessons.title: Teammates and team orders
lessons.objective: Explain why the teammate is the true benchmark and when orders are used.

payload.prompt: Why is the teammate the fairest comparison of a driver?

options.text: Both drivers share the same car, engine and team, so the gap between them mostly shows the drivers.
options.explanation: Right. Rivals in other teams have different cars, so only the teammate is a close like-for-like test.

options.text: The teammate is always slower, so he is easy to beat.
options.explanation: No. Plenty of drivers get beaten by their teammate, which is exactly why the comparison matters.

options.text: Teams give each driver a different car so they can be compared.
options.explanation: The opposite is true. The point is that the car is the same, so one variable is removed.

options.text: The championship leader always gets the faster car.
options.explanation: Teams can favour a driver, but the car is meant to be the same. That is what makes the comparison fair.

explanation.correct: Same car, same tyres, same engine, same pit crew. Almost everything is equal, so the teammate gap is the cleanest read on the driver.
explanation.incorrect: The teammate drives the same car with the same resources, so the gap between them says far more than a comparison with another team's driver.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same car, so the teammate is the real benchmark.

payload.prompt: When does a team typically use team orders?

options.text: When one driver is fighting for the title, or the team needs the points more than it needs a fair fight.
options.explanation: Right. Orders protect a bigger goal: the championship, or the team's total points.

options.text: On every lap, because the boss wants full control.
options.explanation: No. Teams let their drivers race most of the time. Orders are rare and usually for a reason.

options.text: Only at the start of a race, when the lights go out.
options.explanation: Orders can come at any point. They are usually most visible late in a race, when the points are at stake.

options.text: Never, because the rules ban them completely.
options.explanation: The ban was lifted in 2011. Orders are allowed, but teams often get criticised for using them.

explanation.correct: Team orders ask one driver to help the other, to protect a title chance or the team's points. They are rare because they are unpopular.
explanation.incorrect: Team orders are allowed, used sparingly and usually when something bigger than one race is at stake.
explanation.sayThisLine: They used orders because the title fight needed it.

payload.prompt: Why do team orders split fans?

options.text: Some fans want drivers to race freely; others accept orders as part of a team sport.
options.explanation: Right. It is a real difference of opinion, not a rules question.

options.text: Team orders are against the sporting rules.
options.explanation: They are not. Orders are allowed, which is why fans argue about taste rather than legality.

options.text: Orders always cost the team points.
options.explanation: Usually the point of an order is to protect or gain points.

options.text: A driver who obeys an order loses his seat.
options.explanation: Drivers who obey keep their seats. Some are even rewarded later.

explanation.correct: There is no correct side. Purists want a fair fight; others see F1 as a team sport where the constructors' title matters too.
explanation.incorrect: Orders are legal, so the argument is about taste: racing freely versus playing as a team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fair fight or team game? Depends who you ask.

payload.prompt: Your quicker driver is stuck behind his teammate. Do you swap them?

situation.narrative: Lap 30 of 58. Driver A leads his teammate, Driver B, by 1.5 seconds. Driver B says he is quicker and wants to pass. Both are in the points.

facts.label: Driver A
facts.value: Ahead, but losing 0.3 s a lap

facts.label: Nearest rival
facts.value: A rival car is 8 seconds behind

facts.label: Risk
facts.value: They could collide if they fight

options.label: Swap now: let the quicker driver go.
options.consequence: Driver B uses his pace to pull clear, and the team loses no time fighting. Driver A is unhappy for a lap or two.
considerations: The gap to the rival is big enough to protect both cars.
If he is faster anyway, holding him up only wastes time.
Promise Driver A the position back if things change.

options.label: Let them race, but tell them to keep it clean.
options.consequence: They fight. It is entertaining, but each lap of fighting costs both drivers tyre life and risks contact.
considerations: Fans love it and it is fair.
One mistake could cost the team both cars' points.
The rival is 8 seconds back, so there is a little room to race.

options.label: Order Driver B to stay behind, no matter what.
options.consequence: The team loses pace over the stint and Driver B is furious. Driver A's tyres fall away anyway.
considerations: The slower car is holding up the quicker one.
It only makes sense if Driver A has priority for a reason the team has explained.
Driver B may feel the team is protecting the wrong driver.

payload.expertNote: A good team sets its rules for this before the race: who has priority, and when they swap back. Orders land better when the reason is clear and the rule is fair.
payload.sayThisLine: They swapped because he was faster, and they could afford it.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: He got out-qualified by his teammate again. Same car, so he is just slower.

payload.question: Is that the full story?

options.text: It could mean he is slower over one lap, but his race pace might be better. One qualifying does not make him slow.
options.explanation: Right. Qualifying pace and race pace are different. One result is not the whole story.

options.text: Yes, if his teammate is faster in qualifying, he is slower overall.
options.explanation: Not necessarily. Quali and race pace differ. Ask about his Sunday pace too.

options.text: He should just try harder.
options.explanation: Oversimplifies it. Quali and race pace are separate skills; the teammate battle has many laps.

payload.translation: One qualifying result does not define a driver. Some are quick for one lap but slower on race pace, or vice versa. Ask about both.

followUps.why: It matters for the grid, but grid position is not the race. Look at the full weekend and the season.

followUps.line: What is the teammate battle, then?
followUps.why: Comparing both drivers across an entire season: qualis, races, all conditions. One qualifying is a data point, not a verdict.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Do not judge a driver on one result. Ask about his race pace, his consistency and his season total.

lessons.title: The driver pipeline
lessons.objective: Explain F3, F2, super licences, junior programmes and reserves.

payload.prompt: Match each step in a driver's path to F1.

pairs.definition: F3 and F2: junior categories that are the ladder to F1, where drivers prove themselves.
The FIA licence needed to race in F1, earned by accumulating points in lower series.
Team-run academies (Red Bull, Ferrari, Mercedes) that groom and fund young drivers.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty given to drivers who break too many rules.
A special insurance policy for rookie drivers.

explanation.summary: The path is: junior series (F3, F2) → earn a super licence → join a junior programme or fight for a seat → F1.
explanation.sayThisLine: Feeder series earn points for a super licence; junior programmes speed up the journey.

options.text: The FIA licence required to race in Formula 1, earned by scoring points in F2, F3 and other junior series.
options.explanation: Right. You can not race F1 without one.

options.text: A licence you get for free once you turn 18.
options.explanation: No. You earn it by performing in junior series and accumulating super licence points.

options.text: A penalty that stops you from racing in F1.
options.explanation: A super licence is not a penalty; it is the credential to race in F1.

options.text: A certificate of driving ability for road cars.
options.explanation: A super licence is F1-specific. Road cars do not need one.

explanation.correct: Right. A super licence is the FIA document that says you are qualified to race in F1, earned through junior series results.
explanation.incorrect: A super licence is earned, not given. Drivers accumulate points in F2, F3 and lower categories to qualify.
explanation.sayThisLine: You earn a super licence in junior series; F1 requires one.

payload.prompt: What does a junior programme do?

options.text: A team academy funds, trains and grooms young drivers to reach F1; Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes run them.
options.explanation: Right. Junior programmes are talent pipelines that reduce risk for teams.

options.text: A school that teaches teenagers to drive race cars.
options.explanation: Programmes do include training, but they are part of a professional pathway, not education.

options.text: A punishment for young drivers who break F1 rules.
options.explanation: A junior programme is a promotion, not a penalty.

options.text: A lottery that picks random drivers for F1 seats.
options.explanation: Junior programmes are selective. Drivers have to earn their spot.

explanation.correct: Right. A junior programme is a team's way of developing drivers early, nurturing them through feeder series and into F1.
explanation.incorrect: Junior programmes are professional talent pipelines, not schools or lotteries.
explanation.sayThisLine: Junior programmes fund drivers on the way up. Being picked is a big deal.

payload.prompt: Put a typical road to an F1 race seat in order.

items.why: Almost everyone starts in karts, then moves into single-seater categories as a teenager.
These are the ladder to F1, where results and experience are built.
Good finishes in approved series earn the points the FIA requires before a driver can race in F1.

items.text: Reserve or test driver for a team
items.why: Many drivers wait here, stay sharp and learn a team's systems while hoping for a seat.
A seat opens through a retirement, a move or a promotion, and the prepared driver takes it.

explanation.correct: Karts, then F3 and F2, then the super licence points, often a reserve role, then a race seat. Not every driver takes every step, but this is the usual shape.
explanation.incorrect: The usual shape is junior racing, the F3 and F2 ladder, the super licence points, frequently a reserve role, and then a race seat.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is on the ladder: F2 now, reserve next, then a seat.

payload.prompt: Match each role or stage to what it is.

pairs.definition: The main feeder series where drivers prove themselves before F1, step below the world championship.
A driver funded and trained by Red Bull's academy, groomed for Red Bull or sister-team seats.
The third driver at a team, standing by in case the main race driver is unavailable.

distractorDefinitions: A driver who finished second in the championship.
A driver who quit racing to become a broadcaster.

explanation.summary: The path: feeder series (F2, F3) → maybe a junior programme → reserve role → race seat.
explanation.sayThisLine: Feeder series, then junior academy, then reserve, then racing.

lessons.title: Silly season, tifosi and the Netflix effect
lessons.objective: Explain the driver market and how fandom works.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: Silly season has started. Everyone is guessing about next year's seats.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: The driver market: rumours and deals about who will drive for which team next year.
options.explanation: Right. Silly season is when seat moves are guessed at, leaked and finally announced.

options.text: A run of races where drivers keep making mistakes.
options.explanation: Not mistakes on track. It is speculation about contracts and seats.

options.text: A charity event held between races.
options.explanation: Silly season is just the rumour period about driver contracts.

payload.translation: Silly season is the stretch when the driver market heats up: who is staying, who is moving and who is out of a seat for next year.

followUps.line: Why is it called silly season?
followUps.why: Because the rumours fly so fast that half of them turn out to be wrong.
It can. A driver with an uncertain future is under pressure, and a driver who has just signed may be more relaxed.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Silly season stories are often guesses. Asking who is reporting it is a good question.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: The tifosi flooded the track after the race. Monza always goes wild.

payload.question: Who are the tifosi?

options.text: Ferrari's famously passionate fans, especially in Italy. They create incredible atmosphere.
options.explanation: Right. The tifosi are famous for their noise, colour and loyalty.

options.text: All F1 fans around the world.
options.explanation: Tifosi specifically means Ferrari's supporters, not every F1 fan.

options.text: Italian police who manage crowds at the track.
options.explanation: Tifosi are fans, not police. The word is Italian for supporters.

payload.translation: The tifosi are Ferrari's devoted fanbase, strongest in Italy. At Monza they pack the grandstands in red and traditionally pour onto the track after the race.

followUps.line: Why do they flood the track?
followUps.why: It is a long Monza tradition: once the cars are safely back, fans gather beneath the podium to celebrate.

followUps.line: Is Ferrari the only team with passionate fans?
followUps.why: No, but the tifosi are the best known and their colour and noise make Monza unmistakable.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Tifosi are fans, and fandom is part of the sport. Learn the culture, do not judge it.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: F1 has so many new fans thanks to Drive to Survive. The energy is different now.

payload.question: What is Drive to Survive?

options.text: A Netflix series that dramatizes F1 life, paddock politics and driver stories. It brought millions of new fans, especially younger viewers.
options.explanation: Right. Drive to Survive opened F1 to people who never watched before.

options.text: A racing sim game on streaming.
options.explanation: It is a documentary series, not a game.

options.text: The official F1 broadcast on TV.
options.explanation: Drive to Survive is Netflix, independent from F1's broadcast deals.

payload.translation: Drive to Survive is a Netflix documentary series that dramatizes F1 team life, rivalries and driver personalities. It introduced millions to the sport.

followUps.line: Does Drive to Survive show real races?
followUps.why: It mixes race footage with behind-the-scenes drama and interviews. Not every moment is race action.

followUps.line: Do long-time F1 fans like it?
followUps.why: Mixed. Some love the new fans it brings; others find the drama exaggerated. It is a cultural moment either way.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Drive to Survive is entertainment. Real F1 is deeper than Netflix drama, but both matter now.

payload.prompt: In F1, the paddock is where...?

scene.alt: Text only: two meanings of the word paddock.

choices.label: Teams and staff work behind the pits

explanation.correct: The paddock is the backstage area: team motorhomes, hospitality, media and offices. Deals get done and rumours start here.
explanation.incorrect: Fans are in the grandstands. The paddock is the team and media area behind the pits, which is why people say the word when they mean the inside world of F1.
explanation.sayThisLine: That is the talk in the paddock.

payload.prompt: Why do so many fans follow one driver or team?

options.text: Stories and loyalty: rivalries, personalities and a team's history matter as much as who is fastest.
options.explanation: Right. Most fans pick a side for a personal reason, and the season becomes their story.

options.text: Only the team with the most titles is ever followed.
options.explanation: Plenty of fans back small or struggling teams. Loyalty is about the story, not the trophy count.

options.text: Fans are assigned a team by where they live.
options.explanation: Geography can help, like Italy and Ferrari, but people choose by driver, history or family.

options.text: Fans follow whoever won the last race.
options.explanation: Some do, but most stay loyal through bad seasons. That loyalty is the point.

explanation.correct: Fandom in F1 is personal. People pick a driver or team and follow their ups and downs, which is why asking who they support is such a good opener.
explanation.incorrect: Most fans support a driver or team for a personal reason: a family habit, a favourite driver, a first race, a show. It is about the story, not just speed.
explanation.sayThisLine: Who do you support, and how did that start?
